claims.text: The initial material is an as-synthesized HfNbTiVAl10 high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical heterostructure.
The HfNbTiVAl10 heterostructure contains relevant grain boundaries, phase interfaces, and potentially amorphous surface layers.
Tensile strain can be measured using digital image correlation on mechanically tested high-entropy-alloy specimens.
Electron microscopy can provide microstructural information alongside tensile-property measurements in high-entropy or refractory high-entropy alloys.
A machine-learning model trained on mechanical-test data and microstructural descriptors will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture-onset parameters for HfNbTiVAl10.
Machine learning can link alloy descriptors to target elastic properties without running expensive first-principles simulations.
Descriptors of grain boundaries, phase interfaces, and potential amorphous layers mediate the relationship between the HfNbTiVAl10 microstructure and its macroscopic mechanical properties.
The machine-learning model will extract latent correlations between measured microstructural features and macroscopic mechanical properties.
Using the learned correlations will bypass computationally intensive full-scale simulations.
Young's modulus predictions will have approximately 5% error.
Yield-strength predictions will have approximately 8% error.
Fracture-parameter predictions will have approximately 8% error.
Prediction turnaround time will be reduced by at least 40% relative to conventional finite-element simulations.
Conventional finite-element simulations and empirical models for HfNbTiVAl10 require extensive computation and have higher predictive errors than the proposed method.
Temperature and strain rate can materially affect strength and deformation behavior in refractory high-entropy alloys.
The approach should be robust when tensile and fracture behavior is primarily governed by the microstructural features represented in the model inputs.
Environmental degradation, extreme strain rates, or unexpected phase transformations may reduce predictive performance by changing the operative deformation mechanisms.
Incomplete microstructural descriptors or inadequate sampling of heterostructure variability may reduce predictive accuracy.
Failure to meet any of the stated 5% modulus, 8% yield/fracture, or 40% timing thresholds on a blinded independent test set would falsify the conjunctive hypothesis.
